segs.text: Module three, objective two. Steady state, and how it relates to continuous dosing. During an infusion, C p, the plasma concentration, climbs and then levels off. Steady state is that plateau: the rate of drug going in equals the rate going out, so the amount in the body stops changing, and the level there is C s s, the steady state concentration. R, the infusion rate, is an amount per time; the clearance is the volume of plasma emptied of drug per hour; k is the fraction of the drug present removed per hour; and the half-life is the time for the level to change by half.

card.m: steady state: rate in = rate out → C<sub>ss</sub>
R: mg/hr; Cl: L/hr; k: hr<sup>−1</sup>; t<sub>½</sub>: hr

segs.text: Why does the level stop rising? The amount eliminated each hour is the clearance times C p, so early in the infusion, with little drug in the body, little leaves. As C p rises, the amount leaving each hour rises with it, until it equals R. The approach is gradual: the curve comes closer and closer to C s s but in theory never reaches it, so in practice a level close to the plateau is called steady state.

card.m: amount out per hour = Cl × C<sub>p</sub>: small at first
C<sub>p</sub> rises → amount out per hour rises, until it equals R
never reached exactly; close to C<sub>ss</sub> counts as steady state

segs.text: At the plateau, R equals the clearance times C s s, so C s s equals R over clearance. R is on the top, so a higher rate gives a proportionally higher plateau: twice the rate, twice C s s. Clearance is on the bottom, so a patient who clears less drug, for example in renal failure, has a higher plateau on the same rate. V D, the apparent volume of distribution, which relates the amount in the body to C p, is not in R over clearance, so with clearance fixed a larger volume does not change the height of the plateau. C s s equals R over clearance contains no time, so it says nothing about when the plateau arrives.

card.m: R doubled → C<sub>ss</sub> doubled; her review: 50 → 100 mg/hr, 12 → 24 mg/L
Cl falls → C<sub>ss</sub> rises at the same R
e.g. 115.5 mg/hr, Cl 11.55 → 8.55 L/hr: C<sub>ss</sub> 10 → 13.5 mg/L
no V<sub>D</sub> in {{frac:R|Cl}}: V<sub>D</sub> does not set the height

segs.text: How soon the plateau arrives depends only on the half-life. The fraction of C s s reached after infusing for a time t is one minus e to the minus k t, which holds only k and t, so R cannot change the timing. After one half-life the level is half of C s s, after three it is eighty seven point five percent, and after five about ninety seven percent. She said, if I ask you how long it takes to get steady state following I V infusion, the simplest answer is three to five half-lives.

card.m: fraction of C<sub>ss</sub> reached = 1 − e<sup>−kt</sup>: only k and t

segs.text: The half-life depends on the patient: k is the clearance divided by V D, so the half-life, zero point six nine three over k, equals zero point six nine three times V D over the clearance. Clearance is on the bottom, so a smaller clearance, as in renal failure, gives a longer half-life and a slower climb, and on the same rate a higher plateau. V D is on the top, so a larger volume with the same clearance also lengthens the half-life and the climb, while the height stays the same. R is in neither, so the rate changes the height of the plateau and never the time to reach it. She said, It does not change the time that it takes to get to that steady state concentration.

card.m: Cl falls: t<sub>½</sub> longer, slower climb, higher C<sub>ss</sub>
V<sub>D</sub> larger, Cl the same: t<sub>½</sub> longer, same C<sub>ss</sub>
R: the height only, never the time

segs.text: The equation for the rise holds both the height and the timing: C p equals R over clearance, times one minus e to the minus k t. The first factor is C s s, set by R and the clearance; the bracket is the fraction of C s s reached, set by k and t, with t counted from the start of the infusion. Early on the bracket is a small fraction, and near five half-lives it approaches one. Counted in half-lives, the fraction after n half-lives is one minus one half to the power n, so two half-lives give seventy five percent and four give ninety three point seven five percent. About three point three two half-lives reach ninety percent, and four point three two reach ninety five percent.

card.m: (1 − e<sup>−kt</sup>): the fraction reached, the timing

segs.text: Her slide Example four asks how long an infusion must run to reach ninety percent of steady state, with k equal to zero point one five per hour. The fraction of C s s reached, one minus e to the minus k t, answers it, so it is set equal to zero point nine and solved for t. The ten percent of C s s not yet reached is not a power of one half, so the exponential is isolated and t is found with a natural log. The answer is fifteen point three five hours, which she states as about fifteen hours. As a check, the half-life is four point six two hours, so fifteen point three five hours is three point three two half-lives, her ninety percent shortcut.

card.m: t<sub>½</sub> = {{frac:0.693|0.15 hr<sup>−1</sup>}} = 4.62 hr; {{frac:15.35 hr|4.62 hr}} = 3.32 half-lives ✓

segs.text: Her graded quiz asked, Which of the following results when the rate of infusion is increased? The keyed answer is that the steady state concentration increases; the options that the time to steady state increases or decreases are wrong, because the rate sets the height of the plateau and the half-life sets how soon it arrives. Asked how long to steady state, answer three to five half-lives; asked for a stated percentage, calculate it. A renal failure part does change the time, because the half-life is longer: in her Practice three the new steady state takes four point three two of the new half-lives for ninety five percent.

card.m: wrong: the time to steady state increases or decreases
how long? 3 to 5 half-lives; a stated %: calculate
renal failure: 95% at 4.32 of the new, longer half-lives

segs.text: A concentration in the stem can stand for a percentage of C s s. In her Practice four the half-life is six hours and C s s is ten milligrams per liter, so a level of five milligrams per liter is fifty percent, one half-life, six hours. Eighty percent of C s s leaves twenty percent not yet reached, which is not a power of one half, so the log route gives thirteen point nine three hours. Objective six uses this plateau line to choose a rate, and objective five adds a loading dose to skip the wait.

card.m: → R for a target (obj. 6); loading dose, no wait (obj. 5)
